history.heading: Danish West Indies
paragraphs: The United States Virgin Islands, mainly St. Croix, St. Thomas and St. John, lie east of Puerto Rico. They were inhabited by Taíno and Carib peoples before Columbus arrived in 1493. Denmark colonised St. Thomas in 1672, St. John in 1718 and bought St. Croix from France in 1733, forming the Danish West Indies.

Sugar plantations used enslaved Africans. A major slave revolt on St. John in 1733 was suppressed. On St. Croix in 1848, enslaved people led by John Gottlieb ("General Buddhoe") rose up and forced the Danish governor to declare emancipation.

history.heading: American purchase
paragraphs: The United States bought the islands from Denmark in 1917 for 25 million dollars, mainly for strategic reasons during the First World War. Residents became US citizens in 1927. Hurricanes Irma and Maria caused severe damage in 2017.

culture.heading: Island culture
paragraphs: English is official, and Virgin Islands Creole is widely spoken, along with Spanish on St. Croix. Most people are of African descent, and Christianity is central. Danish colonial architecture remains in Charlotte Amalie and Christiansted. Carnival and quelbe music, the official traditional music, are celebrated. About two-thirds of St. John is a national park.

politics.heading: US territory
paragraphs: The US Virgin Islands are an unincorporated, organised territory of the United States. They elect a governor and a single-chamber legislature and send a non-voting delegate to the US House of Representatives. Residents cannot vote in presidential elections.

economy.heading: Tourism
paragraphs: Tourism, including cruise ship visits, is the main industry. Rum production is significant, supported by federal rum tax rebates. A large oil refinery on St. Croix closed in 2012. The currency is the US dollar.
